Opening exercise · 2 of 4
07 / 38

Four lenses for spotting difference.

Captured on the board as the group calls them out. Same four for any pair of articles, anywhere.
01
Tone
Calm vs heightened. Formal vs casual. Reporting vs persuasion.
02
Language
Which words are loaded. Which adjectives appear. What gets called what.
03
Framing
Who's described first. Who's quoted. What context is included, or left out.
04
Emphasis
What's in the headline. What's buried lower down. What never gets said.
Opening exercise · 3 of 4
08 / 38
The takeaway

Bias rarely shows up as outright lies.

What bias is not
Not "they made it up."
Most reporting in mainstream outlets is factually defensible. Each individual claim could be sourced.
What bias is
It shows up in choices.
What to include. What to leave out. Whose voice goes first. How an event is described. Which detail leads. Which is buried.

The leap we're making today
One outlet writing a slanted headline is something. Hundreds of accounts pushing the same slanted framing, on cue, on the same morning, is something else. We'll come back to that in the second half.

For reading any piece of content critically, in five minutes, on your own phone.

Three Habits for Reading Critically
10 / 38
Reusable across the rest of the module

Three habits.

HABIT · 01
Check for previous coverage.
Search the same story across multiple outlets. If only one obscure source is carrying a major claim, that's information.
HABIT · 02
Go to the source.
Track back to the original study, statement, video, document. The distortion often lives in the gap between source and headline.
HABIT · 03
Read around the article.
Investigate the author, the outlet, the wider information environment. Five minutes. Curiosity, not certainty.
You will see these three again Same numbers, same order, every time. Repetition is part of the teaching.
Habit 01 · Previous Coverage
11 / 38
Habit · 01

Check for previous coverage.

If a story is genuinely significant, multiple credible outlets will be covering it.
Walk-through · same headline, three searches
PREMIUM TIMES · TODAY
"FG denies sudden fuel-subsidy reversal, says cited memo is fabricated"
THE GUARDIAN NG · TODAY
"No reversal of subsidy decision, sources clarify"
9JATRENDS24.NG · 4 HRS AGO
"BREAKING: Subsidy returns Monday, secret FEC memo leaked"
Two credible outlets carry the denial. One unfamiliar site carries the "leak". Absence in the mainstream is the signal.
What you're looking for
The story turning up in three or four credible places, Premium Times, Punch, Daily Trust, BBC Pidgin. Not just one. Not just twenty re-shares of the same WhatsApp broadcast.
What it means if it's missing
A "huge" story carried by one unfamiliar blog and nobody else is almost always either niche, exaggerated, or fabricated. Absence is data.
The five-second version
Copy the headline. Paste into Google or check Dubawa. Look at who else is reporting it.
Habit 02 · Go to the Source
12 / 38
Habit · 02

Go to the source.

Most articles report on something, a study, a statement, a video, a document. The original is usually linked or named.
The gap to watch
Between what a source actually says and what an article claims it says, that gap is where information distorts.
What to do
Click the link. Read the paragraph the headline pulled from. Note what the headline added, and what it dropped.
When there's no link
That itself is information. A report on "a new study" with no citation deserves more scepticism than a quiet correction would.
Worked example · headline vs the actual NBS report
THE HEADLINE
"Inflation hits 40%, Nigerians can no longer afford garri, NBS reveals"
WHAT THE NBS BULLETIN ACTUALLY SAYS
Headline inflation: 33.2% (year-on-year). Food inflation in the North-East zone: 40.1%. National food index: 35.4%.
The gap: the article used a regional food figure as the national headline number. The original is one click away. Habit 02 catches this in under a minute.
Habit 03 · Read Around
13 / 38
Habit · 03

Read around the article.

Three things to look at. None requires special tools. All take under a minute.
A
The author
  • Do they exist?
  • What else have they written?
  • What's their record?
B
The outlet
  • When was it founded?
  • Who owns it?
  • What's its editorial position?
C
The wider environment
  • What other coverage exists?
  • Who's responding to it?
  • Where did the claim originate?
The shape of the habit
14 / 38

These are habits, not one-offs.

The size of the commitment
Five minutes. Phone in hand. Multiple times a day.
Not "set aside an evening for investigation". The whole point is that the bar is low enough to clear it casually, in the time you'd otherwise spend doom-scrolling.
The disposition that makes it work
Curiosity, not certainty.
The goal isn't to "prove it's fake". The goal is to know more about what you're looking at than you did sixty seconds ago.

One article. Five minutes. Headline to verdict.

Today's article · projected for the room
NAIJANEWSNOW.ONLINE · YESTERDAY
"Harvard study: 7 in 10 Nigerian youths planning to japa within 24 months"
By "Editorial Desk" · 18k WhatsApp shares
  • Habit 01, a Google search returns the same headline copied across three unfamiliar blogs. Premium Times, Punch, Daily Trust: silent.
  • Habit 02, the "Harvard study" is not on harvard.edu. The closest match is a 2019 Afrobarometer brief on youth migration intent across Africa.
  • Habit 03, "Editorial Desk" has no byline anywhere. The domain was registered 11 weeks ago. Dubawa has flagged a similar claim from the same domain.
  • Verdict in five minutes: not a fabrication, a distortion. Real underlying data, reframed as something it isn't.

Manipulation Tactics · Overview
17 / 38
Second half · the tactics

How content gets engineered to mislead.

Coming up · first
Six tactics that show up again and again.
Each on its own slide, with a Nigerian-context sample, so the pattern is visible rather than abstract.
Coming up · then
How those same tactics scale into propaganda.
Combined. Coordinated. Cross-platform. The move from "misleading post" to "campaign".
None of these are new. They're the same rhetorical and persuasion tactics political operators have used for a hundred years, just running through faster, cheaper, more measurable channels.
Tactic 01 of 06
18 / 38
Tactic · 01

Fearmongering.

TACTIC · 01
Fear
"Severe. Imminent. Personal to you."
Make the consequences feel imminent, severe, and personal, to push the reader past careful judgement.
Fear bypasses analysis. By the time you've thought about whether the claim is true, you've already shared it. That's the whole design.
Sample headline
CIRCULATED ON WHATSAPP
"URGENT: New SIM-registration deadline tomorrow, millions of lines will be disconnected BEFORE THE WEEKEND." Loaded words do the work; the actual NCC announcement was a routine 90-day notice.
Counter-move Notice the pulse-rate change. Slow down. Apply the three habits before reacting.
Tactic 02 of 06
19 / 38
Tactic · 02

Fake experts & credentials.

TACTIC · 02
Expert?
"Borrowed authority. Wrong subject. Out of context."
Authority that doesn't hold up when you look at it.
Three flavours: invented qualifications, real credentials applied to the wrong subject, and genuine experts quoted out of context to support a position they don't actually hold.
Invented
"Dr." with no traceable practice or institution.
Wrong field
Engineering PhD speaking on vaccines.
Out of context
Real quote, cropped to mean the opposite.
Sample byline
FORWARDED CHAIN MESSAGE
"Dr. C. Okonkwo, Senior Consultant, Lagos Institute of Public Health, warns…" A Dubawa search returns no Lagos Institute of Public Health. No registered MDCN number. No published work. The "borrowed" credential is doing all the persuasion.
Tactic 03 of 06
20 / 38
Tactic · 03

Conspiracy framing.

The move
Complex events presented as the work of a hidden coordinated group.
Reality is usually messy, bad incentives, mistakes, structural problems, competing interests. Conspiracy framing replaces that mess with a single hidden actor pulling all the strings.
Why it traps you
Every contradicting fact gets a sinister explanation. Inquiry closes down.
"They would say that, wouldn't they." "Of course there's no evidence, that's how good the cover-up is." Once you're inside the frame, no outside data can reach you.
Tell-tale: a worldview where the powerful are always in coordination, never in conflict, never incompetent, never just unlucky.
Tactic 04 of 06
21 / 38
Tactic · 04

Emotional manipulation.

Content engineered to provoke outrage, disgust, fear, or righteous excitement, because emotional content travels further and faster than neutral content.
Same story · two framings · two outcomes
NEUTRAL
"NERC approves 12% tariff review for Band A customers, citing higher gas costs."
Reach: 4.2k · Shares: 180
OUTRAGE FRAMING
"They've done it AGAIN, FG quietly slips electricity tariff hike past Nigerians while we sleep."
Reach: 380k · Shares: 22k
Same NERC announcement. One word swap, "review" to "hike", and a betrayal verb ("slips past") moves it ~90× further on the feed.
Why it works on you
Emotion compresses the time between "seeing" and "sharing". You react before you've finished reading.
Why it works on the algorithm
Strong reactions = more engagement signals. The system reads "people are responding" and serves it to more people.
Counter-move
If the post made you feel something fast, that's the moment to do the three habits, not to tap share.
Tactic 05 of 06
22 / 38
Tactic · 05

Clickbait & curiosity gaps.

Headlines designed to extract a click by withholding information. Promise far more than the article delivers.
Three Nigerian-feed headlines · what the article actually delivered
"You won't believe what this Big Brother housemate said next…"
→ you would, easily, it's two sentences of small talk
"SHOCKING truth about garri Lagos doctors don't want you to know"
→ article is a recycled blog post on portion sizes
"This Lagos-based banker quit her job, what she's doing now will surprise you"
→ she sells small chops · the surprise is not surprising
The reveal almost never matches the size of the promise. That gap is the business model.
Why it works
A curiosity gap is uncomfortable. The brain wants the gap closed, even if the answer is trivial.
What it costs you
Your time, your data, and the slow training of expecting reality to deliver "shocking truths" every scroll.
Tell-tale
If the headline could be answered in one word and isn't, that's the gap.
Tactic 06 of 06
23 / 38
Tactic · 06

False equivalence.

The move
Two sides presented as equally weighted when the evidence behind them isn't.
"Balanced coverage" that gives the same screen time to a position with mountains of evidence and a position with almost none. The visual symmetry hides the asymmetry of the actual data.
Watch for "Some say… others say…" with no weighing of who is right and on what.
Why it matters
Lends unearned legitimacy to fringe positions.
A fringe claim placed next to a mainstream finding is a fringe claim that has just inherited the visual authority of "this is one of two reasonable sides".
A useful ask "What's the actual weight of evidence on each side here?"
From tactics to campaigns
24 / 38
04

The propaganda
landscape.

The six tactics aren't only used by individual creators chasing engagement. They're also the building blocks of organised propaganda, the same moves, combined at scale.
Four shapes to recognise
25 → 28
Shape 01 of 04 · Coordinated Inauthentic Behaviour
25 / 38
Shape · 01

Coordinated inauthentic behaviour.

Networks of fake accounts and bots. Amplify content to make a position look more popular, or more contested, than it actually is.
A swarm, most "voices" are not people
Inauthentic / amplifier Real account
What it makes you feel
"Everyone agrees with this." Or, sometimes, "this is enormously contested." Both can be manufactured.
Tell-tales
Accounts with no history before this month. Identical posting times. Generic profile pictures. Near-identical bios.
Documented case
Stanford Internet Observatory's 2020 take-down of a Nigeria-linked network: ~270 accounts running coordinated pro-government and anti-opposition hashtags around the #EndSARS period. Catalogued by Dubawa and DFRLab.
Shape 02 of 04 · Narrative Laundering
26 / 38
Shape · 02

Narrative laundering.

A claim starts somewhere unreliable, gets picked up by something slightly more mainstream, and eventually appears in respectable coverage with its origins stripped out.
STAGE · 01
Fringe origin
A claim, "FG plans to ban Bolt and Uber in Lagos by Q3", goes up on an anonymous Telegram channel and a freshly-registered .ng blog.
→
STAGE · 02
Pickup & amplification
A partisan aggregator writes it up: "Reports suggest FG considering Bolt and Uber ban." Cites the Telegram post. Frames it as plausible enough to discuss.
→
STAGE · 03
Reputable response
A mainstream outlet runs "Drivers' union reacts to ride-hailing ban reports", quoting the aggregator's coverage, not the original Telegram post.
→
STAGE · 04
Origins stripped
By the next news cycle, it's "as reported earlier this week, plans for a ride-hailing ban…" The Telegram origin is no longer visible.
The point: by stage 04, a claim that started on a Telegram channel now wears the clothes of credible reporting. Habit 02, go to the source, is what walks it back.
Shape 03 of 04 · Astroturfing
27 / 38
Shape · 03

Astroturfing.

Organised activity dressed up as a spontaneous grassroots reaction. Stock language. Template comments. Repeated across many accounts.
Sample · comments under a single post
@user_71203 · 14:02
"Absolutely outrageous. Concerned parents will not stand for this."
@user_71412 · 14:03
"Outrageous! Concerned parents will not stand for this."
@user_71588 · 14:03
"Absolutely outrageous! Concerned parents will not stand for this."
@user_71601 · 14:05
"Hmm, this seems badly framed. Anyone got the original?"
@user_71777 · 14:06
"Concerned parents will absolutely not stand for this. Outrageous."
@user_71891 · 14:07
"Outrageous! As a concerned parent I will not stand for this."
Highlighted comments share near-identical phrasing, timing, and account-naming pattern.
What it tries to manufacture
The impression of an organic mass reaction, to give a campaign the moral weight of "ordinary people are upset".
Tell-tales
Repeated phrasing. Suspiciously similar usernames. Accounts that never post about anything else.
Why it matters
"Spontaneous public outrage" is a powerful political signal. Faking it short-circuits the democratic process the signal is meant to reflect.
Shape 04 of 04 · Influence Operations
28 / 38
Shape · 04

Influence operations.

Media manipulation as a tool of foreign policy, political competition, or commercial interest. State actors. Non-state actors. Sometimes both at once.
A
State actors
National governments running media-manipulation operations against domestic populations, foreign populations, or both, often through cut-outs that don't visibly carry state branding.
B
Non-state actors
Political campaigns, commercial PR firms, ideological movements, and contract operators-for-hire, running the same playbooks, often with the same suppliers.
C
Both at once
A state hires a private firm; the firm rents from a contractor; the contractor uses the same bot network it sold to a corporate client last quarter. The lines aren't clean, and aren't meant to be.
Worth knowing You probably can't fully attribute a campaign on your own. You can recognise that one is happening.
The key principle
29 / 38
The principle this module rests on

Recognising propaganda is not the
same as agreeing or disagreeing
with a political position.

It's seeing when content has been engineered, by whom, and why.

Exercise · Reference Example
31 / 38
What 'good' looks like

Plausible. Emotional. Lightly sourced. Hard to scroll past.

EXAMPLE
NAIJA PULSE 247
Breaking · Today · Lagos
EXCLUSIVE: Lagos secondary school SECRETLY trialling controversial new policy, parents kept in the dark, experts "deeply concerned"
An unnamed source close to the principal said the move would "fundamentally change school life by third term". Anonymous parents from the school's WhatsApp group described the situation as "outrageous" and "a betrayal of trust".
No member of staff has confirmed the policy publicly. No circular has been seen. A respected educationalist, "Dr. M. Adeyemi", with credentials in an unrelated field, said it raises "serious questions for every Nigerian parent". The full picture remains unclear, but those briefed described it as…
By "Education Desk" · naijapulse247.example.ng
Tactics labelled in the margins
T1
Fearmongering, "SECRETLY", "fundamentally change", "betrayal".
T2
Fake expert, "Dr. Adeyemi" credentialed in an unrelated field; not in any MDCN or NUC register.
T3
Emotional manipulation, outrage, betrayal, parental anxiety stacked.
T4
Clickbait headline, withholds the actual policy, promises a reveal.
T5
Anonymous sources, every concrete claim is one WhatsApp-group step removed.
